JBPA management
High-level architecture
Customer-deployable architecture

JBPA Management
Platform

A dependable path from AI request to governed delivery, isolated execution and a durable result.

Purpose

Automate Private Agent lifecycle actions on named, supported hosts.

Architecture

Jitterbit MCP, API Manager, Studio and JBMQ connect to a dedicated management API, worker and PostgreSQL database.

Customer reuse

One versioned Linux container package, with customer-specific configuration and a matching Harmony integration kit.

Read the architecture in this order

From the operating problem to a deployable and supportable product.

1. Understand the solution - pages 3 to 6

The constraints, deployment boundaries, component responsibilities and an example installation establish what the product does.

2. Follow one job - pages 7 to 9

Three sequence diagrams explain submission, execution and result retrieval. Every message is tied to an actual component and a durable job identity.

3. Understand the choices - pages 10 to 16

Technology selection explains why each part is needed, the value it adds, the open-source reuse model and what remains customer-specific.

4. Define the contracts - pages 17 to 22

The Jitterbit project, tools/APIs, job model, queue semantics, security and onboarding describe how the system is implemented.

5. Operate and qualify it - pages 23 to 29

Failure recovery, deployment, upgrades, availability, acceptance criteria and references complete the lifecycle.

Jitterbit | Proposed design v3.0 | 06 October 20262 / 29
JBPA management
High-level architecture
Architecture / 03

The problem and the design boundaries

Manage a named agent reliably without depending on that agent to run its own management service.

Why a management product is needed

Private Agent lifecycle actions can take several minutes and can restart or remove the target runtime. An AI tool call needs a prompt acceptance response, a stable job identity and a result that can be retrieved later.

What the customer deploys

A dedicated Linux management host runs the JBPA API, background worker, database and HTTPS proxy in containers. A reusable Harmony project exposes protected APIs and uses JBMQ to deliver execution requests.

What stays on target hosts

The existing SSH service provides access. JBPA runs its verified lifecycle commands and retains execution evidence on the target. No new web server, daemon, container or listening port is added to the PA hosts.

Scope and ownership

JBPA manages pre-provisioned, supported hosts. Target VM provisioning, customer identity/network configuration and Harmony record deletion remain separate responsibilities. Each customer runs an independent product deployment.

The target is selected from the approved inventory. It is never selected by whichever management PA happens to execute a Studio operation.

Who does what

Every layer has a specific responsibility; the management API remains usable without an AI client.

LayerResponsibilityValue added
AI client + Jitterbit MCPDiscover named tools, submit actions and retrieve jobsA natural-language interface backed by structured contracts
APIM + StudioProtect the API facade; validate/map requests; publish and dispatchReusable integration project and private-network reach through management PAs
JBMQBuffer references waiting for execution acceptanceDecouples delivery from execution and tolerates dispatch interruptions
Parent API + PostgreSQLAuthorize requests; persist jobs, outbox and resultsOne authoritative answer from acceptance through completion
Background worker + JBPACoordinate targets and execute fixed remote actionsLifecycle execution survives API-process restarts
Target host + HarmonyInstall/run the PA and supply observed health/registration evidenceActual runtime outcome, distinct from delivery acceptance

Management PAs and target PAs are different roles

Any eligible management PA may dispatch the request to the same parent endpoint. The dedicated parent resolves the requested target. A target PA can be offline or absent and still be managed over SSH. [J2]

JBPA management
High-level architecture
Architecture / 06

One installation, from request to result

Example: install the approved agent version on the named target qa-pa-03.

StepWhat happensWhat is durable
1. RequestThe client calls jbpa_install with target, exact version and idempotency keyClient retains the request identity
2. AcceptAPIM/Studio asks the parent to create the jobJob and publication-outbox entry commit together
3. DeliverStudio sends the job reference to JBMQQueue message exists; publication is recorded separately
4. DispatchThe dispatcher asks the parent to accept execution, then ACKs JBMQJob is READY before delivery acknowledgement
5. ExecuteWorker acquires host ownership and runs JBPA through SSHAttempt identity, evidence location and execution state
6. RetrieveThe client later calls jbpa_get_job through APIMStored outcome with target/version/evidence correlation
Accepted is not installed. An installation is successful only when the required JBPA outcome checks pass. A repeated same-identity request returns the same job.

JBPA management
High-level architecture
Architecture / 07

Sequence 1 - accept and publish

The first HTTP call finishes after durable acceptance; installation has not started.

A job and outbox record are committed atomically before acceptance. If publication is interrupted, a scheduled Studio relay retries the pending outbox item. Duplicates are expected and safe.

Jitterbit | Proposed design v3.0 | 06 October 20267 / 29
JBPA management
High-level architecture
Architecture / 08

Sequence 2 - dispatch and execute

A queue message is acknowledged after the parent accepts execution, not after installation finishes.

The dispatcher makes a short acceptance call. The independent worker performs the minutes-long SSH action and persists its result. Lost dispatch responses reuse the same job ID.

Architecture / 09

Sequence 3 - retrieve the result

Status retrieval is a new tool call that reads the job record.

The AI may poll if its client supports it, or the user can ask later. Jobs finish independently of the conversation. Automatic chat resumption must be verified for each supported client.

JBPA management
High-level architecture
Architecture / 11

API technology - reuse the Python investment

FastAPI defines the contract; the separate worker owns long-running execution.

Python + existing JBPA

WHY: the repository already contains lifecycle adapters, release validation and a structured SSH caller.
VALUE: wrapping the fixed caller preserves its checks instead of duplicating install logic.
REUSE: API and worker share request/result models and one application image. Other clients can use the same REST API.
TRADEOFF: remote attempt recovery and a production execution profile still require code changes.

FastAPI + Pydantic

WHY: typed request/response models support validation and OpenAPI/JSON Schema generation. [T1, T2]
VALUE: reject invalid target/action/version input early and keep Jitterbit transformations aligned with the API.
REUSE: model definitions become documentation, tests and client schemas.
TRADEOFF: validation is not authorization; action/target checks remain application responsibilities.

Uvicorn + separate worker

WHY: Uvicorn serves the ASGI API; a separate process claims durable READY jobs.
VALUE: API restarts do not erase accepted execution work.
REUSE: the same worker image can run with different permitted inventories.
TRADEOFF: process restart does not prove a remote mutation stopped; reconcile its original attempt.

Alternatives considered

Flask can serve this API but needs more explicit schema integration. Node.js/Go would introduce another language around a Python execution engine. FastAPI in-memory background tasks are insufficient as the durable job mechanism. A new Celery/Redis stack is not required for the initial product.

Jitterbit | Proposed design v3.0 | 06 October 202611 / 29
JBPA management
High-level architecture
Architecture / 12

Database technology - durability and coordination

PostgreSQL is selected for the product baseline, including customers with more than one worker.

PostgreSQL

WHY: transactional creation of job + outbox, uniqueness for idempotency, and controlled concurrent claims. [T3]
VALUE: results and ownership survive application restarts; uncertain actions remain visible.
REUSE: customers can use the bundled DB or a qualified external PostgreSQL service.
TRADEOFF: backups, migrations and restoration are required operations.

Worker ownership

WHY: a queue can redeliver and a worker can fail mid-installation.
VALUE: canonical-host ownership prevents simultaneous lifecycle changes across aliases and workers.
REUSE: the same contract works for one worker or a qualified expanded deployment.
TRADEOFF: lease expiry is only a warning; it never independently authorizes replay.

SQLAlchemy + Alembic

WHY: explicit transactions and schema changes tracked as released migrations.
VALUE: every customer can upgrade through a tested version sequence.
REUSE: application repositories, migration tests and database compatibility checks are shared product code.
TRADEOFF: migrations must be reviewed and run once; database portability is not promised merely by using an ORM.

Why not SQLite or another broker?

SQLite fits a small local tool, but PostgreSQL is the deliberate shared-service baseline for this product. JBMQ already handles external delivery; the parent database holds accepted worker jobs. A second broker would add deployment and recovery responsibilities without a demonstrated requirement.

Architecture / 13

Packaging technology - portable and replaceable

The deployment framework reduces customer setup; it does not replace operational ownership.

Docker Engine + Compose

WHY: the service topology is bounded and customers requested Linux containers.
VALUE: pinned images, service networks, health checks and persistent volumes make installation reproducible.
REUSE: the same release runs in each qualified customer environment.
TRADEOFF: Compose is a single-host baseline; Docker Desktop and Kubernetes are not prerequisites. [T4, L9-L11]

NGINX Open Source

WHY: provide a standard TLS entry point separately from application code.
VALUE: centralize certificates, request limits and proxy routing; keep API/DB ports internal.
REUSE: customers may substitute their existing qualified gateway without changing the API.
TRADEOFF: certificate lifecycle and trusted proxy headers need explicit configuration. [L8]

OpenSSH + the existing caller

WHY: the target already has an established remote administration interface.
VALUE: encrypted access and pinned host identity without adding a PA-host web service.
REUSE: the worker delegates to the existing inventory-based caller rather than building a new transport.
TRADEOFF: credentials, sudo access and interrupted-command evidence must be governed. [L12]

Keep the default deployment bounded

Kubernetes introduces a control plane and operational skills that the first customer package does not require. Managed PostgreSQL and existing reverse proxies are optional integration profiles. Redis/Celery remain unnecessary until a specific worker capability cannot be satisfied by the durable job contract.

What can be reused across customers

A standard product package contains the code; each deployment supplies its own infrastructure and identity.

Reusable product assetCustomer-specific configurationBoundary
API/worker images and schemasDeployment ID, limits, retention and API URLNo customer source-code fork
Compose manifests and deployment checksLinux host, DNS, TLS and persistent-storage locationNo claim that every Linux distribution is qualified
Jitterbit project and MCP definitionsTenant/environment, security profiles, queue IDs and endpoint variablesLicensed Harmony resources are still required
Target execution adapterHost inventory, pinned keys, SSH identity references and maintenance permissionsTarget VM provisioning remains external
Migration/backup/recovery toolingBackup destination, credential recovery and agreed recovery objectivesOperational evidence is per deployment
Tests, docs and release manifestCustomer onboarding and support ownershipSupport matrix governs what is promised

Open-source components versus our own code

The API design is reusable through HTTP/OpenAPI and the packaged runtime can be self-hosted. No repository LICENSE file was identified in the current JBPA checkout. Publishing our own code as open source therefore requires an explicit license/ownership decision. Jitterbit binaries, branding, credentials and vendor artifacts are not automatically covered by upstream component licenses.

Docker licensing boundary

The deployment uses Linux Docker Engine and Compose. Docker Desktop is a separate product with subscription terms; it is not a customer runtime prerequisite. Registry access, support, host infrastructure and Jitterbit licensing remain costs to assess. [L9-L11]

The reusable Jitterbit project

Short operations provide the submission, delivery and status facade.

OperationTriggerRequired behavior
Submit JobAPIMValidate; create parent job/outbox; attempt queue publish; return job and observed state
Relay Pending DispatchScheduleClaim pending outbox entries; publish references; mark confirmation after successful send
Dispatch JobSchedule + JBMQ GetRead reference; ask parent to accept; ACK accepted/duplicate job
Get Job / List TargetsAPIMQuery the parent; preserve permitted status and safe evidence
Delivery RecoveryOperator / scheduleClassify undeliverable references; bounded delayed retry or quarantine
Notify CompletionOptional scheduleSend configured notification once; does not promise chat resumption

Why APIM and Studio add value in this design

APIM exposes the supported contract; Studio carries credentials, mappings and queue orchestration. Management PAs bridge the customer network to the private parent endpoint. JBMQ makes delivery asynchronous. A forwarding-only project would add little value, but the queue/relay/status project has a defined role. [J1-J3]

Every management PA uses the same parent URL. Harmony routing selects an execution agent, while the parent inventory selects the lifecycle target.

MCP tools and API surface

Keep business tools understandable while sharing one versioned parent contract.

MCP capabilityBusiness inputsParent behavior
Install / upgradetarget, exact qualified version, idempotency keyPOST /v1/jobs creates/retrieves durable job
Uninstalltarget, idempotency keyQueue local removal; Harmony record deletion separate
Status / health / versionstarget, idempotency keySame async pattern for predictable timeout behavior
Get jobjobIdGET /v1/jobs/{jobId} reads retained state/result
List targetsNo host/address inputGET /v1/targets returns permitted targets only

Tool configuration

Use the provided Jitterbit MCP server editor: name/description, REST method/endpoint/path, request/response schemas and backend authentication. Resources provide prerequisites/support information; templates provide guided workflows. Production behavior must be validated in the actual tenant.

Client-visible contract

Return 202 only after durable acceptance, 200 for retrieved results, a stable job ID and honest current state. Expose equivalent errors through APIM: invalid input, unauthenticated, forbidden, not found, conflict and dependency unavailable. Response body alone must never imply installation success.

Jitterbit | Proposed design v3.0 | 06 October 202618 / 29
JBPA management
High-level architecture
Architecture / 19

Jobs, events and execution state

The database answers what was accepted, what ran and what evidence was retained.

RecordPurposeKey constraints
JobCaller, target, action, request hash, versions, state, resultUnique idempotency scope; inventory revision and canonical host
Event / auditTransitions, execution attempt and authorization decisionsOrdered safe history; access-controlled retention
Dispatch outboxRequired queue publication and confirmationCreated with job; replay-safe publication
Host ownershipActive job/attempt, heartbeat and reconciliation stateOne mutation per canonical host; alias-safe
Evidence referenceNormalized result and protected detailed evidence IDSecret-free API result; checksummed restricted evidence
Migration recordApplication/database compatibilityControlled schema version

Execution lifecycle

ACCEPTED_PENDING_DISPATCH -> READY -> RUNNING -> SUCCEEDED or FAILED. An uncertain remote outcome enters NEEDS_RECONCILIATION while host ownership is retained. Queue publication is recorded separately and cannot regress a running or completed job.

Idempotency and results

Same key + same canonical request returns the same job. Same key + changed parameters is a conflict. Diagnostic status does not prove identity-aware Harmony health. Requested/resolved versions, artifact digest, worker release and attempt identity support reproducible diagnosis.

Jitterbit | Proposed design v3.0 | 06 October 202619 / 29

High-level architecture
Architecture / 20

Queue reliability and publication recovery

The request queue buffers delivery; the parent database preserves the business record.

SituationDesign response
Job commit succeeds; queue send failsKeep outbox entry; relay republishes later
Queue send succeeds; publication acknowledgement is lostRepublish if necessary; parent suppresses duplicate execution
Parent accepts dispatch; Studio loses responseRedeliver same job; parent returns existing accepted state
Known lifecycle failureStore FAILED result; do not treat it as queue transport failure
Invalid or unauthorized messageQuarantine/dead-letter; never execute command data from the envelope
Messages age or queue reaches capacityAlert; preserve outbox/job state; reconcile and republish when appropriate

Acknowledgement and retry

ACK only after the parent commits READY or confirms compatible prior acceptance. Use bounded delayed retry. Do not wait for installation before ACK. The queue design must respect the customer tier and avoid assuming additional retry queues are licensed. [J1, J4]

Service constraints

JBMQ documents a 30-minute acknowledgement timeout and a maximum message TTL of 10 days. Monitor backlog and oldest job; PostgreSQL is the historical source. New submissions require the parent and DB because durable job creation precedes queue publication. [J1]

High-level architecture
Architecture / 21

Security and network access

Protect the business request, the service identities and the privileged remote execution.

ConnectionControlSecret/data boundary
AI -> Jitterbit MCPSupported authenticated client and allowed toolsNo tokens or SSH material in prompts
MCP -> APIMConfigured security profile and backend authenticationJitterbit API credentials managed in tenant
Studio -> parentPrivate HTTPS; issuer/audience/expiry/signature checksScoped machine token; TLS trust validation
Parent -> databaseRestricted role and internal networkJob/results omit secret values
Worker -> targetPinned host key, fixed caller, permitted action/targetSSH identity only mounted to worker
Target -> Harmony/downloadsApproved outbound endpoints and staged credentialsProtected on-target registration file

Identity is enforced in the service

A shared integration identity receives only its explicit scope. Delegated user identity must be verified, not trusted from model-generated headers. Separate submit, relay, dispatch, read and administrative permissions. Rotate access tokens, TLS and SSH material through tested procedures.

Container and evidence isolation

No privileged containers or Docker socket mounts. Only HTTPS is published on the management host; API/DB stay internal. Compose secret mounts are protected files, not encryption or a vault. Logs/results are allowlisted and redacted; detailed vendor evidence is restricted.

Architecture / 22

Onboard a target before enabling mutations

Host identity and support qualification are explicit parts of the customer configuration.

StepCustomer / product actionVerification
1. PrepareCustomer provisions supported VM and network routesOS/architecture/capacity match supported tuple
2. IdentifyAssign canonical host ID and target nameAliases cannot create separate mutation ownership
3. Pin accessIndependently verify fingerprint; configure SSH identityStrict host-key checking and approved login
4. Stage secretsCustomer secret mechanism supplies protected registration fileInventory contains only the remote path
5. ValidateCheck configuration, sudo, routing and artifact/version policyNon-mutating preflight report
6. AuthorizeEnable permitted actions and maintenance policyQualified install/upgrade edge; observed expected identity

Versions and action boundaries

Pin a qualified package/digest and caller release. Do not silently turn install into upgrade/reinstall. Complete local uninstall leaves Harmony record management separate. Mutable latest and unsupported tuples are rejected unless a separately governed qualification mode explicitly permits them.

Mapping revisions

A job records the inventory revision used at acceptance. If a target mapping changes, execute against the approved recorded mapping or reject/reconcile the job. Never redirect a queued job to a new host silently. [R2-R4]

Jitterbit | Proposed design v3.0 | 06 October 202622 / 29
JBPA management
High-level architecture
Architecture / 23

Recover safely when execution is interrupted

A timeout means the outcome may be unknown; it does not mean the target is unchanged.

Failure boundaryRequired recovery behavior
Before remote startEstablish non-start from attempt evidence before resuming
SSH loss during mutationRetain host ownership; inspect original attempt/process/result
Worker crash / expired heartbeatFence abandoned attempt; do not launch a second mutation solely on lease expiry
DB failure after remote changePreserve safe local/remote evidence and reconcile before new work
Management host loss / DB restoreStop dispatch; restore; fence workers; reconcile active jobs and stale queue references
Resolved installation failureServe structured failure; new lifecycle action requires its own authorization

Required adapter improvement

Before any mutation, bind a stable job/attempt identity to the remote command and evidence path. The current synchronous caller discovers some evidence after execution; the product must make interrupted attempts discoverable through SSH without adding a target daemon or port.

Execution guarantee

Delivery is at least once and requests are idempotent. Exactly-once remote mutation is not claimed. Safety is provided by canonical-host coordination, remote locking, stable evidence and reconciliation. Generic executing-job cancellation and package rollback are excluded until qualified.

Deploy the same package for each customer

Configuration changes per customer; source code and release images remain the same.

Package contents

Pinned API/worker images; Compose manifests; configuration schemas; database migrations; backup/restore and upgrade tools; target-access validator; version/support matrix; Jitterbit project kit; smoke tests and operator runbooks.

Deployment automation limits

Container portability does not imply every Linux host is supported. Publish tested distribution/architecture/runtime versions. Use actual Harmony export/import interfaces; retain explicit manual setup steps where automation is not available. A clean-host deployment must pass before claiming easy repeatable installation.

Architecture / 25

Upgrade, back up and restore the product

Management-product upgrades and target-agent upgrades have separate authorization and evidence.

OperationRequired procedureProduct value
Build/releasePinned dependencies/images; SBOM; notices; provenance; compatibility manifestReproducible customer package and supply-chain traceability
Management upgradePause new dispatch; safely drain; backup; migrate once; deploy; verify; reconcile; resumeTested repeatable version path
PA upgradeSubmit explicit target job with qualified old/new package edgePreserves separation from management deployment
BackupEncrypted off-host DB/config/evidence backup; recoverable secret referencesRecovery independent of the management host
RestoreFence workers; restore schema/data; recover keys; inspect remote attempts; resume cautiouslyNo blind replay of a pre-crash mutation
RollbackUse only tested application/schema recovery pathsNo generic DB downgrade or package rollback promise

Release ownership

Keep customer secrets out of images, manifests and queue messages. Publish dependency/runtime support windows and security update guidance. An image rollback is safe only when schema and active-job compatibility are proven.

Recovery objectives

Agree recovery point/time objectives with each deployment and measure restore drills. A backup file is not proof of successful restoration. Use PostgreSQL-supported backup mechanisms; a future managed DB profile can share the same API/worker contract. [T5]

Jitterbit | Proposed design v3.0 | 06 October 202625 / 29
JBPA management
High-level architecture
Architecture / 26

Operate the service and scale deliberately

A recoverable single-host baseline supports the first product release; availability claims require evidence.

Operational signalWhat it detectsOwner action
Outbox age / queue backlog / DLQDelivery interruption or capacity pressureRepair relay/dispatch; reconcile references
READY age / worker heartbeatWorker capacity or abandoned executionInspect workers and host ownership
Reconciliation count / action durationUncertain outcomes and lifecycle bottlenecksInspect original remote evidence
API/DB readiness / storage / backup ageInfrastructure health and recoverabilityRepair dependencies; verify restoration
Version/attempt correlation and auditUnsupported combinations or denied actionsReview policy, release and access decisions

Capacity and availability

Benchmark concurrency against target download/installation times, SSH load and DB persistence. Configure bounded worker limits; one mutation per host remains mandatory. Compose restarts processes but cannot survive host loss without recovery. HA requires redundant application hosts, HA PostgreSQL, shared evidence and proven fencing.

Support model

Product engineering owns released code and compatibility evidence. Customer operations owns hosting, backups and routes. Harmony administrators own queues/projects/licensing. Identity administrators own credential policy. Recovery operators own documented reconciliation decisions.

Appendix - contract examples

Illustrative payloads show the separation between acceptance and execution results.

Create job

POST /v1/jobs
Authorization: Bearer <machine token>
Idempotency-Key: <stable request UUID>

{"target":"qa-pa-03",
"action":"install",
"version":"12.10"}

202 Accepted
{"jobId":"<job UUID>",
"state":"ACCEPTED_PENDING_DISPATCH",
"target":"qa-pa-03"}

Retrieve result

GET /v1/jobs/<job UUID>

200 OK
{"jobId":"<job UUID>",
"state":"SUCCEEDED",
"target":"qa-pa-03",
"action":"install",
"requestedVersion":"12.10",
"resolvedVersion":"12.10.1.1",
"result":{"status":"SUCCESS"}}

Queue envelope and internal routes

Queue: {"schemaVersion":1,"jobId":"<job UUID>"}

Scoped parent APIs:
GET /v1/dispatch-outbox
POST /v1/dispatch-outbox/{id}/published
POST /v1/jobs/{id}/dispatch
GET /v1/targets
GET /health/live and /health/ready

Error and state semantics

400/422 invalid input; 401 unauthenticated; 403 forbidden; 404 unknown/not-visible job; 409 conflicting identity/request; 503 dependency unavailable.

READY means accepted for execution. RUNNING means an attempt exists. NEEDS_RECONCILIATION means the original remote outcome must be inspected. Samples are proposed, not observed output.
